title: tenant-chaos-gaming-and-resilience-onboarding-playbook-2026
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview:

This playbook defines the tenant-level chaos gaming and synthetic-resilience program used during enterprise onboarding and the first 90 days post-cutover. It standardizes simulated failure scenarios, telemetry assertions, success criteria, and escalation steps to validate that a new tenant meets Redwood Inference stability, performance, and cost-safety requirements prior to and immediately after canary-to-100% rollouts.

Purpose and scope:

- Purpose: Reduce production surprises by exercising realistic failure modes against a customer’s dedicated or private deployment in a controlled, observable way.
- Scope: Applies to Dedicated and Private tenants (VPC/on-prem) being onboarded or undergoing major model/capacity cutovers. Does not replace load testing performed by SRE for platform-wide capacity.

Service-level targets (tenant SLOs):

- Availability SLO: 99.95% for API success rate (5xx and client-facing errors excluded per contract).
- Median latency target: <120ms for small-gen calls (<128 tokens) during canary windows.
- Cost safety guardrail: 2x expected cost spike tolerance during orchestrated synthetic tests; anything beyond triggers immediate throttling.

Owners and contacts:

- Playbook owner: Customer Success (Aisha Patel)
- Runtime escalation owner: Eng SRE (Miguel Ramos)
- Dedicated/private deployment owner: Eng Private Deployments (Jordan Lee)
- Customer POC: (fill per customer onboarding sheet)

Prerequisites (before running a game day):

1. Tenant must be deployed to a non-prod or canary tenant slice with identical routing, or to a production tenant with explicit consent and an agreed blast radius.
2. Observability contract validated: metrics, traces, and logs forwarded to Redwood telemetry cluster and customer-observability link.
3. Canary token/key configured and QA test suite green.
4. Rollback and safe-failover plans approved by customer and SRE.

Game day checklist (pre-execution):

- Schedule and obtain approvals from customer, SRE, and account team (minimum 72 hours notice).
- Configure synthetic load generator (see examples below) and ensure isolation of test traffic via label/filter.
- Snapshot current tenant config and telemetry baseline (last 24h).
- Confirm cost cap and automatic throttles are active.
- Run a brief smoke test of observability dashboards and alerting rules.

Synthetic scenarios (recommended list):

1) KV-cache corruption simulation
   - Intent: Ensure graceful detection and refetch behavior for prefix cache invalidation.
   - Method: Inject cache-miss pattern by toggling a feature flag in the canary runtime to disable cached lookup for 60s.
   - Success criteria: Error budget unaffected; latency increase <50% for affected requests; automated PK cache warm-up completes within 120s.

2) Model-variant fallback under load
   - Intent: Validate model fallback routing if primary quantized model fails or is cyclically unavailable.
   - Method: Simulate model-worker OOM by marking worker pool unhealthy via the orchestration API.
   - Success criteria: Requests routed to fallback variant within 10s; tail latency spike limited to 2x baseline for under 5 minutes.

3) Sudden traffic surge from one tenant (ingress storm)
   - Intent: Confirm tenant fairshare and quota protector sidecar behavior.
   - Method: Generate a 10x RPS spike for 5 minutes using synthetic generator.
   - Success criteria: No cross-tenant degradation; affected tenant receives throttling with appropriate 429s and customer-notification webhook triggers.

4) Telemetry pipeline delay and partial loss
   - Intent: Ensure offline buffering and alerting are robust when telemetry forwarding lags.
   - Method: Introduce deliberate forwarding latency in the staging observability forwarder for 3 minutes.
   - Success criteria: Alerts that depend on telemetry use alternative guard signals (health check pings); post-mortem shows no blind spots longer than 5 minutes.

Execution play (numbered runbook):

1. Kickoff: Confirm attendees and intent. Document start time in the incident timeline channel.
2. Baseline sampling: Start 5m metric sampling to baseline key telemetry (request_rate, error_rate, p50/p95 latency, cost_per_minute).
3. Scenario run: Execute scenario steps as defined. One scenario per 15–30 minute window.
4. Observability watch: SRE and CS watch dashboards for SLO violations. Assign a single comms owner.
5. Containment: If a hard threshold is crossed (see thresholds table), immediately stop the synthetic generator and trigger rollback if needed.
6. Cooldown: 15–30 minutes post-scenario for caches and queues to settle. Collect logs and traces.
7. Post-checks: Run validation tests (sanity generations, embedding consistency checks).

Thresholds and automated actions (table represented in plain text):

- If 5xx rate > 0.5% for >2 minutes -> Automated throttle and page SRE (Pager).
- If median latency > 3x baseline for >5 minutes -> Pause canary rollouts and create severity-3 incident.
- If cost rate > 3x baseline sustained >10 minutes -> Trigger cost-protector webhook and notify finance-safety.

Telemetry assertions (examples to add to the telemetry contract):

- request.success_rate >= 99.5% (rolling 10m)
- model.fallback.count <= 5 per 10m window during synthetic tests
- cache.hit_ratio >= 70% post-warmup (rolling 5m)
- ingress.rps <= documented expectation for the tenant + 10% burst allowance

Observability queries (examples):

- Error rate: sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant=\"<TENANT>\",status=~\"5..\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant=\"<TENANT>\"}[5m]))
- Median latency: histogram_quantile(0.5, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket{tenant=\"<TENANT>\"}[5m])) by (le))

Synthetic load generator examples:

- k6 (simple RPS spike)
  - Command: k6 run --vus 0 --iteration-duration 5m --rps 200 spike-script.js
  - Note: Use request headers to tag traffic: {\"X-Tenant-Test\":\"chaos-game-2026\"}

- locust (ramp test):
  - Command: locust -f locustfile.py --headless -u 500 -r 50 --run-time 10m --host=https://tenant.example

Rollback and safe-failover steps:

1. Stop synthetic generators immediately.
2. If degradation is tenant-isolated and within cost guardrails, hold and let cooldown complete.
3. If cross-tenant impact or severity thresholds exceeded, perform automatic fairshare enforcement and execute configured rollback (model pin to previous stable version).

Post-game day analysis (deliverables):

- Short RCAs for any threshold breach (published within 3 business days).
- Telemetry snapshot and comparison to baseline (attach to the onboarding ticket).
- Action items with owners and target completion dates (tracked in JIRA).

QBR & onboarding handoff checklist:

- Add game day results to the QBR packet: include pass/fail per scenario, regression deltas for p95, and cost delta.
- Recommend final tenant readiness vote (Accept / Accept with mitigations / Reject) during the commercial go/no-go.

Appendix A — Example alerting rule YAML (snippet):

alert: TenantHigh5xx
expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant=\"<TENANT>\",status=~\"5..\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant=\"<TENANT>\"}[5m])) > 0.005
for: 2m
labels:
  severity: page
annotations:
  summary: "High 5xx rate for tenant <TENANT>"
  runbook: "/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/incident-process"

Appendix B — Tracing play snippet:

- When a scenario runs, add a trace tag: chaos.game=tenant-onboard-<ID> so Perf and Trace teams can filter.

Appendix C — Postmortem template fields to include:

- Timeline of actions (UTC)
- What failed vs expected
- Root cause and contributing factors
- Immediate mitigations and permanent fixes
- Customer impact and communications

Frequently asked questions:

Q: Can we run game days against production?
A: Only with explicit customer written consent and a pre-negotiated blast radius. Use a dedicated canary slice where possible.

Q: Who authorizes rollbacks?
A: SRE owns urgent rollbacks; CS must be informed within 15 minutes for customer-facing incidents.
